svg.title: Designing a day with breathing room

text.tspan: Everyday English - B2 - 2026/10/12 - Essay - 01
A calendar gives plans a place in time.
Pexels · 20657557
Designing a day with breathing room
A meaningful schedule needs more than a full calendar. Protecting valued activities and leaving gaps between commitments can
create the breathing room needed for sustained attention.
First, protecting one priority makes it easier to act on what matters. I made a deliberate adjustment by setting aside time to read
before opening my messages. Some replies had to wait, but reading finally became part of my day rather than a postponed intention.
Second, small gaps prevent commitments from competing for every available minute. I began leaving a short break after meetings
instead of scheduling another task immediately. That pause helped me recognise when I was spreading myself too thin and adjust the
rest of the day.
Protected priorities and deliberate gaps both make attention more sustainable. Neither requires a completely empty calendar; each
requires accepting limits. I now judge my schedule by the room it gives meaningful activities, as well as the tasks it contains.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each
body paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a
new proposal.
Identify two obstacles that could arise when people make a realistic plan. Explain a workable response to each, rather than merely
listing the problems. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion. (Model: One possible outline:
introduce the situation; discuss reviewing a specific experience teaches more than a vague judgement with an example; discuss a
small next step is easier to act on than a broad promise with a different example; conclude by connecting the two points.)
